### Proposition 40

#### BILLIONAIRE TAX

Prop 40 would tax extreme wealth to help meet urgent needs, but its one-time structure conflicts with principles of sound public finance and risks long-term revenue loss.

The federal government is walking away from feeding people and providing access to basic health care, putting Medi-Cal coverage and CalFresh benefits at risk for millions of Californians. When it does, the state has a responsibility to step in. Prop 40 would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on billionaire wealth. The state would direct 90% of the revenue to health care, with the remaining 10% going to education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. That could deliver tens of billions to the safety net when families are losing both.

The measure also confronts a deeper problem the League cannot ignore. The wealthiest American households pay a lower total effective tax rate than the whole population, largely because business wealth produces little taxable income. As of September 2025, roughly 900 American billionaires held nearly double the wealth of the entire bottom half of the country. Inequality on that scale demands that solutions like wealth taxes get serious consideration.

On the con side, Prop 40 makes budget decisions at the ballot box, locking the proceeds into an earmarked fund. The Legislature could choose how to spend within those categories but could not redirect the money to other needs. A one-time tax is also only a stopgap for programs that need funding every year. Furthermore, the tax rests on only a few hundred people. Of these, six billionaires reportedly left the state before the January 1, 2026, cutoff, potentially erasing more than one-quarter of the proponents’ projected $100 billion revenue. It should be noted that the government estimates only tens of billions of dollars raised over several years and says the amount is highly uncertain. The government also estimates that state revenue could be reduced by less than $1 billion per year.

The deeper fear is behavioral: that the tax pushes billionaires out after they pay and deters others from ever coming. The government offers only the broad estimate that state revenue could be reduced by below $1 billion per year. On the other hand, some research finds that tax-driven migration among the wealthy is modest, and Silicon Valley’s ecosystem is not easily traded away.

The human need is urgent and asking those most able to pay to fill a hole the federal government created is a fair demand. But the tax mechanism limits legislative flexibility for allocating money where it is most crucial and raises the risk of taxpayer flight. Because we have strong positions on both sides of this measure, the League takes a neutral position on Prop 40.

### Proposition 41

#### LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES & REQUIRES SPECIAL TAX AUDITS

Prop 41 would put revenue from new state taxes under the Gann Limit’s rigid constitutional spending cap, making it harder to fund essential services and respond to changing needs. It would apply to any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026.

The League opposed the Gann Initiative in 1979 because its spending limit was too inflexible to assure adequate government services in an uncertain future. Prop 41 would extend that constraint to new tax revenue. This is especially concerning for voter-approved initiatives, which generally cannot be changed by the Legislature without another vote of the people.

Prop 41 would also require audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes, including programs such as public campaign financing that may not receive General Fund support. If a new tax excluded its revenue from the Gann Limit, the state could not impose, collect, or enforce it. The audits would add state costs, estimated by the Legislative Analyst’s Office in the low millions of dollars annually and growing over time. It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.

[Proposition 41](https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its [cousin initiative Prop 42](https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.

Backed by Building a Better California, [a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin](https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund. 

What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?

Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.

The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution. 

Known as [the Gann Limit](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.

Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.

Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.” 

We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.

Consider California’s [Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently [exempt from the Gann Limit](https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted [Prop 52 in 2016](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016). 

But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.

California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse. 

Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”

But they’re largely redundant and would *decrease* efficiency. 

Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already [assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.  

The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.
